title: Energy security in volatile times | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Live Energy Gang episode from ADIPEC 2026: the Middle East conflict and disrupted Gulf exports have made energy security the dominant theme. Guests from Pertamina Hulu Energy, KBR and InterContinental Energy discuss supply diversification, plant resilience, the gas-ammonia-food link, data centres outbidding grid-powered hydrogen, and a possible decade of higher energy prices.

themes.theme: Gulf conflict makes security the top priority

insights.claim: The conflict in the Middle East and disruption to exports from the Gulf region made energy security the dominant issue at ADIPEC 2026 in Abu Dhabi.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Policy and capital allocation are pivoting from transition framing toward supply security.
insights.quote: The conflict in the Middle East has made energy security the dominant issue at this year’s ADIPEC
insights.locator: The conflict in the Middle East

insights.claim: Energy systems were already under strain before the Gulf export disruption, following a series of shocks including Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Cumulative shocks mean little spare resilience in global energy systems.
insights.locator: The conflict in the Middle East

insights.claim: Alex Tancock of InterContinental Energy argues the world has underinvested in energy supply and mismanaged policy for at least a decade, and the Gulf conflict simply brought forward a crisis that was coming anyway.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Suggests the supply tightness is structural, not a transient war premium.
insights.quote: the conflict in the Gulf simply brought forward a crisis that was coming anyway

insights.claim: Alex Tancock, with Pertamina Hulu Energy's Dannif Danusaputro agreeing, expects the world may be heading for a decade of higher energy prices driven by supply disruption, which may spur the investment needed to bring prices down again.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A long higher-price regime favours upstream producers and supply-side capex plays.
insights.quote: we may be heading for a decade of higher energy prices driven by supply disruption

insights.claim: Host Ed Crooks concludes the world may be only at the beginning of an energy crisis whose full implications will take a long time to emerge.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Second-order effects of the Gulf disruption are not yet priced.

insights.claim: Indonesia uses about 1.6 million barrels of oil per day but produces only about 600,000 barrels per day, according to Pertamina Hulu Energy's Dannif Danusaputro.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A ~1 mb/d import gap makes Indonesia highly exposed to Gulf supply shocks.
insights.locator: Dannif explains the challenge facing Indonesia

insights.claim: Securing physical oil supplies has become a national priority for Indonesia, and Pertamina Hulu Energy is focused on diversification and partnerships to develop new resources.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Expect more Indonesian upstream partnership deals and farm-ins.
insights.locator: Dannif explains the challenge facing Indonesia

insights.claim: Indonesia is reducing reliance on imported oil through transport electrification, but cannot rely only on EV growth and must work on oil supply as well as demand.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: EV adoption in emerging Asia complements rather than replaces oil supply investment.
insights.locator: Dannif explains the challenge facing Indonesia

insights.claim: KBR has had to adapt quickly to help Middle East customers keep plants running safely through the crisis, rethinking spare parts, local supply chains and capacity to repair damaged facilities.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Crisis drives demand for engineering services, repair capacity and localised supply chains in the Gulf.

insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Resilience-by-design may raise capex per plant but create new engineering revenue.

insights.claim: Rising natural gas prices threaten food supplies because ammonia produced from natural gas is essential to fertiliser production, linking energy and food security.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Gas price shocks transmit to fertiliser and food inflation, a macro second-order effect.
insights.quote: Energy and food security are linked, because ammonia produced from natural gas is essential to fertiliser production.

themes.theme: Desert renewable hubs vs data-centre power demand

insights.claim: InterContinental Energy's desert renewable hubs, combining strong night wind and daytime sun, reach a capacity factor of 74% before any storage.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Hybrid wind-solar siting can deliver near-baseload renewable output, lowering firming costs.
insights.quote: giving a capacity factor of 74% before any storage

insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Sub-$3/kg green hydrogen claim, if real, would be competitive; and data-centre power is an alternative revenue stream.
